Re your point [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] “Explain that we currently do not block riders for a low rating and this does not affect anything for riders” → I wouldn’t say it doesn’t affect the riders (because it does - low rated riders do get less trips). I’d simply say that *we* don’t take any corrective/punitive measures (such as blocking) against riders. 



{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Bias and accuracy*
{panel}

First things first - it is very important to stress that the objectivity of the rating has nothing to do with data accuracy. While I acknowledge that the rider can perceive the situation differently then the driver, who submitted the feedback, it’s generally not subject to assessment on whether it’s correct/accurate, as it’s an opinion.

We have taken this into account when performing the Rider Rating LIA ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1mfPz6423uwRmP0sbMnzpmf2Igb3hAAiu/edit#heading=h.iazupcz0it3t]). While the angle we took regarding bias is a bit different from the point that the rider is making; but the main points regarding ratings and comments are:

* Ratings and feedback are inherently subjective, reflecting personal experiences and perceptions rather than factual data. Accuracy pertains to factual information, while opinions or perceptions, by nature, vary and are not required to be "accurate" in the same sense.
* Feedback and ratings reflect individual viewpoints, which are naturally influenced by personal experiences and perceptions. This subjectivity is unavoidable but allows for a broader understanding of user behaviour.
* Allowing drivers and riders to express opinions promotes a safer platform, as feedback can help highlight behaviours that may compromise safety, even if perceptions differ between parties.
* Riders are expected to follow Marketplace Conduct Guidelines ([https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|smart-link]) to help maintain a safe, respectful environment for both riders and drivers. These guidelines clarify expected behaviour from riders.
* We’re not in the car with the driver and the passenger, so we can’t know what’s happening there. Therefore, opinions shared by drivers and riders help us monitor and enhance service quality, identify potential issues, and create an environment that values both parties’ perspectives.



To sum up - yes, we considered this aspect; unfortunately, that’s how comments and ratings work - while we want for it to be as objective as possible (and we do so through codifying expected behaviour through Marketplace Guidelines), it’s impossible to avoid bias. I can leave a 1* to seller on eBay simply because I think the jacket they sold me is hideous 🙂 and that’s my opinion, which is biased by nature.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

Hi [~accountid:5ed4b18fc3b5390c24a6f905] , thanks for submitting this!

From a privacy standpoint, the disclosure of personal information about the driver to the fleet owner requires a *clear legal basis* (i.e. _determine what empowers us to share it - legitimate interest to protect the fleet’s property could be a potential option_) and should follow *data minimization principles* (a.k.a _share only what’s needed_) to protect the driver’s privacy while addressing the fleet owner’s interest. 

+*Here are my initial thoughts:*+

* Given that the fleet owner has a legitimate interest in assessing potential risks to their property, it may be justifiable to provide a summary or categorization of incidents without disclosing full details. This could include anonymized or aggregated information about the nature of the safety cases (e.g., “damage to vehicle” or “behavioral concerns”) without sharing specifics that could identify the driver or passenger directly.
* If possible, anonymizing the information further (e.g., by sharing incident types or general safety categories) may meet the fleet owner’s needs without disclosing the driver’s personal data.

+*As mentioned, we are required to share only what’s necessary - so, my questions are:*+

* Could you specify what details the fleet owner is asking for? What data do they need from us?
* Has the driver been informed about this potential disclosure to the fleet owner? It’d be good to know if we already reached out to the driver and perhaps he said “no” to his data being shared.

I had a look at the event and *as it is* it can only be done in low risk markets. This does not really differ from campaigns we had globally. However I can’t green light this initiative on a global level.
Concrete feedback:

* wording is not optimal (we don’t use wording like “top performing drivers, quality controls, to increase quality etc.)
* creating cohorts could be seen as critical, what does this mean? The initiative should be available and accessible to *all drivers starting from zero*
* No automated opt-in or at least sufficient information how to opt-out
* these are all low value perks which are fine (please don’t promise a car)
* KPIs need to be discussed on a local level (we won’t have DS anymore, KPIs are subject to local counsels especially for any kind of high risk markets)
* for high risk markets the same applies such as for Bolt Rewards: the only KPI which we can use are *the number of finished rides*, no DS no ratings
* We always need T&Cs for such initiatives
* any marketing and PR communication needs to be reviewed as we need to be careful with the wording and what we are communicating publicly
* We have done something similar in a couple of markets such as NL,DE, UK which we have called “driver league”, “super league” etc. Found old T&Cs which were used for NL here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Sf3S2W8ybxJqrvgpRILvbxB0Sns9lk-H/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Sf3S2W8ybxJqrvgpRILvbxB0Sns9lk-H/edit|smart-link] ,PT Super League announcements from the past: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1D9uTl6QuMjWTkKWf9NEtjOhxytEZ0KLdwY4wf9_rmYg/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1D9uTl6QuMjWTkKWf9NEtjOhxytEZ0KLdwY4wf9_rmYg/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link]

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *15 October 2024.*



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 



As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software. Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail, we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.



We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Tax Reports*



For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/sk-sk/privacy/|https://bolt.eu/sk-sk/privacy/|smart-link] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.



*Your rights* 



In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.





Yours sincerely,



Bolt

There does not seem to be any way to set options/modifiers out of stock in the “reject order due to out of stock” process. Only the full menu items are choosable there. So the assumption is that providers are specifically going into the menu options or Provider Portal and setting the relevant options to out of stock.



From our team’s side, we could, *in the Provider App*, block marking an individual option as out of stock if this change would completely prevent ordering a menu item. But since modifiers can be shared between modifier groups, we would have to full scan the menu.

For this reason, I believe it would make more sense to run this logic on the backend side. Hey, [~accountid:712020:1c2aa130-d609-49b9-a3b0-7eda790d4a4b]. Thank you for your request! 

With the changes to low/moderate event handling, fault determination and event confirmation have become more manual processes as the tool is no longer there to suggest the outcome. The 🚨🚗 [Rides Safety case handling workflow for Low/moderate events|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/47156?country=global&language=en] article contains step-by-step instructions for solving low/moderate safety events from beginning to end, including how to determine the fault. 

For no-tool markets, the applicable guidelines for determining fault are covered in *Step 3: Investigate the case:* 

* You check how many previous reports related to the same event grouping the reported party has _(considering demerit decay)_. 
* You need to take into account the Event Confirmation and number of precedents together with the current event, so you need to review the reported party’s profile and previous safety case Admin comments. 
* You proceed through the steps, and you end up with Event Confirmation and Fault Determination. 
* Afterwards, you follow the Blocking Matrix _(can be found in the 🚨🚗_ [_Safety: guidelines for Low/moderate events_|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/50085?country=global&language=en#blocking-matrix-solving-the-safety-event] _article)_ to determine the Consequential Action based on the results of your investigation. 
* It is also important to consider all the reported user’s precedents that highlight a pattern of behaviour *despite the Grouping*. The reported party’s profile needs to be viewed as a whole, and if the user is, in general, a good or bad actor, we should take it into consideration when answering the question of whether the Consequential Action suggested by the Blocking Matrix is appropriate.

If we take your example where we have *Event CBC* and *Fault CBC*, but it is the driver’s 3rd report of the same grouping, then you apply the relevant consequential action depending on demerit decay _(which is 3 months for low/moderate events)_. So, in this case, it would either be a warning or a 1-day suspension. 

I hope this answers your question. 🙏 

I will be closing this ticket, but if something is still unclear or if I have misunderstood anything, please do not hesitate to reach out in this ticket. 

Wishing you a nice day! 🙂

Thank you for escalating to Customer Payments team. The customers don't always have a great visibility when the pre-authorization has been returned to them. Returning the pre-authorization is not something Bolt has much control over. 
Depending on the bank the pre-authorization charges can take up to a month to be returned to the customer. 
If the Authorization state is Captured then everything is fine on our side and the customer has to check with their bank. 

Please only escalate the issue to Payment Operations team if

1. The funds have not been returned after 30 days and customer has checked with their bank

2. The state has been stuck in authorization for more than 24 hours. (72h for Micro Mobility) 

3. The state of the authorization is failed or error. 

Please leave a comment on the ticket if you still want it to be escalated to the Customer Payments team. Else the ticket will be closed in 5 days.

Hey [~accountid:6108e65ceb7aef0069e5ba05]  ,

In order to create base fee calculators, we would need the following information:

* *Commission rate*: Commission percentage that will apply per ride to the driver/fleet.
* *Currency*: Usually country default if not stated otherwise
* *Invoicing strategy*: Driver or Company. This will define to whom payouts will go, and invoices will be issued.
* *Cash-blocking thresholds*: Defines the cash ride limits for blocking/unblocking cash rides for a driver. This can be copied from other cities, but please discuss with [{color:#b3f5ff}Billing Analytics{color}|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/3/group/1240/create/806] if your market is cash-heavy.
** Max negative balance before messaging: The threshold where we will notify the driver that they are getting closer to being cash-blocked
** Max negative balance before removing cash payments: The debt threshold we allow cash rides up to. After the driver exceeds this threshold, cash orders will be disabled.
** Minimal balance to unblock cash rides: The balance threshold where we will once again unblock the driver’s cash rides.
* *List of company_ids you want this fee calculator to be attached to*.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*What is a Base Fee Calculator*

It is a default fee calculator template created by Billing team in order for local operations teams to easily attach the relevant fee calculator to new companies. [Please read this guide to see how|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/1603928517/Base+fee+calculators].
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
Make sure to make such requests at least 3 days in advance to have buffer for gathering this information
{panel}

_Before the hackathon we had ChatGPT integrated into Beehive and wanted to understand its benefits. ChatGPT had access to the chat history and case data available in Beehive). Access to admin and knowledge base was not given._
_This is what agents were able to do with it:_

* _Translating the chat history (the translated text would show additionally under each text bubble)._ 
* _Create a summary of the chat history_
* _Writing prompts within Beehive._

*Translation of chat history*

*   *Observation*: The translation feature was loved by agents for rides. In Lithuania rides agents receive many tickets from Russian speaking drivers. Since agents dont speak Russian, they are asked to translate the text using google translate (chrome extension) and write a response in English. Often drivers would continue writing in Russian.
* *To Improve:* The two things we saw was a) the translations would massively enhance the chat history (doubling the amount of text in the window), making it difficult especially for longer chats, and b) ChatGPT is very slow and often agents thought the translation button doesnt work because it was loading forever.
* *Solution:* a) redesign how agents see translations.{color:#ff991f} instead of showing both languages, we would just show the translated text. {color}However, in case a ticket contains multiple languages and an agent speaks one of them, we show the language the text was translated from and give the possibility to show the original text message by elapsing the text bubble.
* *Next steps:* Currently {color:#ff991f}replacing ChatGPT with Google translate{color} (from Comms team) for better performance. {color:#ff991f}After that, get buy in from CS and test in a few markets.{color}

*Create a chat summary*

*    *Observation*: Initially agents were mistrusting the summary of the chat created by ChatGPT. However, after a few cases agents saw that it actually works and found it helpful especially for cases that had a long chat history and were already touched by multiple agents.
* *Next steps*: Improve the design and{color:#ff991f} implement a button within Beehive to create a case summary {color}and test it with a larger audience. {color:#ff991f}ETA tbd.{color}

*Writing prompts*

*   *Observation*: It is too hard to control what ChatGPT does. Agents asked what should be the next step and ChatGPT comes up with a solution that is not aligned with our guidelines. The only clear use case identified by agents was to rephrase messages sent by agents. Customers would often respond and be very stubborn which leads agents to state the same response as before but just in different words. Here ChatGPT can help.
* *Next steps*: {color:#ff991f}Dump the prompt idea and focus on concrete use cases for ChatGPT {color}where we have more control over what chatgpt is supposed to do. We will focus building an {color:#ff991f}action button for rephrasing text only{color} and test it with a larger audience. {color:#ff991f}ETA tbd.{color}

*Internal summary on the recent DPA review:*

We are progressing towards alignment; however, further clarifications was requested from MQ on a few newly introduced provisions in the latest iteration of the DPA.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
Below is a summary of our key points of concern flagged to MQ:

* *Use of Anonymised data*: MQ would like to include this but does not clarify how exactly it intends to use aggregated and anonymized data in its operations. This remains a concern, and we requested further clarifications.
* *Processing for MQ own purposes*: we cannot agree to MQ processing personal data for its own purposes of product or service improvement. Subject to alignment on clause 2.6, data processing aimed at product or service improvement may potentially be limited to anonymized and aggregated data.
* *Obligations towards Bolt re/ assistance to MQ (processor) with their processing obligations with Issuing Banks*: while the clause introduces quite basic requirements that should not be difficult for Bolt to comply with (i.e. Bolt undertakes to assist with DPIAs), the use case for this clause remains unclear, as does the rationale for its inclusion at this stage.
* *On-site audits (Clause 6.2)*: We agreed to on-site audits in line with MSA provisions, pending alignment with Bolt’s audit suggestions in the MSA.
* *Limitation of Liability (LoL) and Indemnity*: privacy will negotiate the LoL and indemnity clauses within the MSA regarding privacy violations.
* *Term and Termination Provisions*: we requested to retain the DPA termination provisions, as they complement those in the MSA.
{panel}

Hi [~accountid:6271119d76b8d3006872899e]. They are depicted like that because transportation services are taxed in the country where the service was performed. Bolt Poland cannot on our Polish invoice break down the amount into net and VAT of such foreign cost where local VAT was added. The transportation services that were provided for example in Hungary were taxed there (as you saw local VAT was added), they are not falling in scope of Polish VAT at all (that’s why we don’t calculate any VAT on our invoice), we recover the total (gross) cost. If the Client wants to seek some additional explanations please suggest him to contact his own tax advisors, accountants.

*For your info*: What we do is we recover from the Client the total cost we paid for this, for example, Hungarian ride. There is no possibility to deduct in Poland Hungarian VAT (and also VAT from any other country, so neither we as Bolt nor our client could just add this foreign VAT to its Polish VAT return). Generally such costs are therefore treated as a whole (also with this locally added VAT) as tax cost and for this purpose the line on the invoice is sufficient. If Client reaches out to his advisors, accountants, they will know.

h2. *Wrong address communication test analysis*

[https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NDRKUYQ3/p1731585033880669|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NDRKUYQ3/p1731585033880669|smart-link] 

Hi - [here’s|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZGDkKkO73nnLPfaHYdW-sfP5sDxKY7zaniOghOX1f_Y/edit?tab=t.0] the analysis of the test.

* As a result of more aggressive warnings on the potentially wrong address, the proportion of sessions receiving the warning increased from 4.1% (control) to 9.4% (treatment). However, despite receiving the warning on the home screen, treated users are similarly likely to see warnings on the checkout page (10.5% v. 10.2%). Overall, *the proportion of sessions where the address was changed increased only slightly, from 9.7% (control) to 10.0% (treatment) of sessions* and *the proportion of orders with a change in address sometime during the session increased from 16.3% to 16.5%.*
* We observe a decline in CS tickets associated with treated users; eater-initiated CS tickets decline for reasons of ‘order not delivered’ and ‘edit delivery address’, bringing down potential CS costs by roughly 45K EUR per year. Meanwhile, courier-initiated CS tickets decline for the reasons of ‘unable to contact customer’ and ‘incorrect customer location’, bringing down potential CS costs by 42K EUR. *This results in reduced annual CS costs by 87K EUR.*
* There is no detectable difference in the courier time from courier arrival to order delivered, indicating likely no improvements in this part of the experience.



h4. Why is the Impact Relative Low?

Overall, the impact is quite small, given the small scope of CS impact and no change in courier time.

Among controlled users who already received a potentially wrong address warning on checkout, we see that the proportion of sessions where the address is changed following the warning is 26.2%, and not much higher for treated users (27.3%). Additionally, among controlled users, those who do not change their address following the warning are as likely as those who change their address to raise CS tickets for any reason. *This may point to limited opportunity scope here.*

We tested ECU FW 39 (MPC 7 and MPC 0) vs. ECU FW 3F in Zurich with Alcino Major. All scooters were equipped with IOT ZK115 FW2305.


||*Scooter*||*ECU FW / MPC*||*Flat Road (0% gradient) 50m*||*Hilly Road (6% gradient) 200m*||
|320-331|ECU FW39 MPC 0|Max speed: 20Km/h , 0 to 20: 9 seconds|Max speed: *9Km/h*, 0 to 8: 3 seconds, 0 to 9: 10 seconds|
|292-285|ECU FW39 MPC 0|Max speed: 20Km/h , 0 to 20: 9 seconds|Max speed: *9Km/h*, 0 to 8: 3 seconds, 0 to 9: 10 seconds|
|491-320|ECU FW39 MPC 7
Note: With a rider weight of 70 kg, the difference is very noticeable. This scooter felt very torquey and had no problem climbing a 6% grade hill from a standstill. In contrast, the other scooters with the MPC 0 felt very weak. I believe that if an 80 kg rider attempts to climb even a 5% gradient, they may encounter difficulty.|Max speed: 20Km/h , 0 to 20: 4 seconds|Max speed: 19Km/h, 0 to 19: 6 seconds|
|762-506|ECU FW3F MPC 0
felt almost no difference from the 491-320, overall good torque.|Max speed: 21Km/h , 0 to 20: 4 seconds|Max speed: 19Km/h, 0 to 19: 8 seconds|
|188-475|ECU FW3F MPC 0
again same result as the 762-506, good torque overall|Max speed: 21Km/h , 0 to 20: 4 seconds|Max speed: 19Km/h, 0 to 19: 9 seconds|

Based on the results above, we are confident on updating 50% of the ES600 Berlin Fleet to ECU FW3F MPC 0.

Alcino also reported that he could feel the dynamic configuration adjusting the motor on the flat road thus the reduced noise, and also turning the motor completely off on the downhill.

Dear [{color:#ff5630}*name*{color}],

Thank you for raising your questions regarding the information provided to you about passengers. We take privacy and regulatory compliance very seriously, and we’d like to clarify our approach to sharing passenger information in line with privacy laws.

As you may know, the EU General Data Protection Regulation ('GDPR') requires us to adhere to key principles, including _purpose limitation_ and _data minimization_. This means that we are legally obligated to share only the minimum amount of personal data necessary for a given purpose - in this case, the completion of the journey. Sharing additional or “full” information about passengers would not be necessary to fulfill the journey and, as a result, would go against GDPR requirements.

In addition, our [General Terms: Drivers|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/legal/tnc-general-terms-drivers/?category=rides] do not envisage sharing “full information” about passengers; rather, they specify that we will share “_information relevant to the fulfilment of the Journey_” (see clause 16.2). This means that the passenger information provided to you is specifically curated to enable you to successfully and safely complete each journey.

Our approach ensures both compliance with privacy obligations and protection of all parties.

Thank you again for reaching out with your question. If you have further concerns or need additional clarification, please don’t hesitate to contact us.

Adding here some context from Jevgeni: 

* The attendance data that he shared is based on whether the wifi was connected to the laptop during the day or not. It does not specify the number of signals, meaning that even if only 1 signal was sent, the employee is marked as present. Of course, the person would not know when the signal is sent. For example, I go to the office, open the laptop, the wifi signal was sent, I close the laptop and go home after an hour. Even though I was at the office for an hour only, I'm marked as present. On the contrary, it can be that I'm at the office for an hour, but wasn't 'lucky' enough for the laptop to send the signal, and I get marked as absent.
* If the laptop is closed, e,g. I'm at a workshop at the office the entire day but never open my laptop, I'll be marked as absent.
* *The current wording in the Employee Privacy Notice is not correct, as the signals are not collected every 3 minutes.* More interestingly, we don't know how often it's done, only that it's approximately every hour (Jevgeni was able to confirm this by looking at the available data).
** *Is it possible to check the exact frequency?* Very unlikely, as it depends on the laptop and the hotspot (hotspot = devices at the office that collect the signal that the laptop sends). If needed, Jevgeni said it could be checked with the vendors, but as I understood it, it's not that simple as multiple vendors are included, etc.
** *Is it possible to configure a certain frequency ourselves at Bolt?* Maybe, but he can't promise anything. He said that if we say it's needed, he will look into it.
** Where did the 3 minutes come from then? Not sure, as the data was entirely managed by InfoSec previously, something was configured differently probably.
** The most accurate wording for now is that the signal is checked on average once per hour.
* He also shared absence data in the channel. This is completely unrelated to wifi signals and comes from Workday instead (e.g. the person is marked as on sick leave, on vacation, etc). For example, if the employee is on sick leave but comes to the office for the entire day, they would still be marked as present.
** The absence data is checked because if the employee has not been marked as present for the entire week, it will be checked whether they were absent (i.e. on leave according to Workday) or not - if yes, it means they have a reason for not going to the office.

on installs.i_af_id = ftr.ftr_af_id

* [PoC Flow Diagram|https://www.figma.com/board/oGeZ4x4Gw6wCe2XmulPcXS/dbt-metircs-PoC-flow?node-id=0-1&t=v6Y1rqIY43X3SfZc-1] (use the Figma password saved in our team’s 1Password group).

* [XP RH metric groups spreadsheet|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1wWDrPInawj-Q9eia10KGC85D78iOjF1heRlZO0ATtng/edit?usp=sharing] (RH Metric Groups page).
* [DBT Metrics spreadsheet|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1MMEKS5yY0DCmE4IDHxQCkqK3No4mlySUogyykUaJBi8/edit?usp=sharing].

h3. Key Takeaways

* Our current metrics can be split into *three groups* based on their {{count_expression}}:
** {{green}}: very simple metrics where the aggregators are calculated as {{SUM(metric)}}, {{SUM(POWER(metric), 2)}}, {{COUNT(metric)}}.
** {{yellow}}: simple metrics with the same straightforward sum and square sum definition, but with the count expression being defined as {{COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)}}.
** {{red}}: complex metrics where data and count expressions can involve different metrics; for instance, {{avg_user_spend}}.
* All metric definitions will live in DBT. These definitions contain additional parameters used by AB Processor defined inside the {{meta.ab_processor}} parameter.
** For our current {{green}} and {{yellow}} metric groups, we only require the *original dbt metric definition* + the definition of the {{meta.ab_processor.agg}} parameter. This parameter is used for test/user-level aggregation when composing XP Denormalized Table. 
** For our current {{red}} metric group, we have to have the *original dbt metric definition* used for data expression, and the *count* *dbt metric definition* that also defines a count expression. Both these metrics have to have the {{meta.ab_processor.agg}} parameter defined.
** For *simple* dbt metrics, the {{meta.ab_processor.agg}} parameter can be either taken from the Semantic Model, or defined explicitly. For the *derived* dbt metrics, this parameter has to be *defined explicitly* because the source metrics our metric derives from can have different aggregations.
** The Experimentation team *does not own* the metrics, only uses them.
* All XP metric (aggregator) definitions *only reference the dbt metric*.
** We can have our custom parameters defined there as we do currently. However, everything that relates to metric calculation has to be defined in dbt.
** We can also consider moving all the parameter definitions to dbt. Thus, getting rid of XP aggregator definition.
* MetricFlow is used to generate the query that combines all the necessary dbt metrics for the test.
** This can be a standalone component; it can be a generated dbt model, a separate job, etc.
* The user enrollments table is a separate incremental dbt model.
* The resulted MetricFlow query is joined with user enrollments on the randomization unit.
** The query is grouped by the randomization unit, test ID, and test slicers.
** The metrics are thus aggregated using their respective {{meta.ab_processor.agg}} dbt parameter.
* The *resulted joined query* is then fed to AB Processor along with the *parsed dbt metric definitions* joined with their respective *XP aggregator definitions* to then be used for the sum, squared sum, and count expressions calculation.

This approach is validated via the simple PoC implementation. The implementation results are mentioned here: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/jira/software/projects/XP/boards/525?selectedIssue=XP-2088|https://taxify.atlassian.net/jira/software/projects/XP/boards/525?selectedIssue=XP-2088|smart-link].

Hi, [~accountid:628dd71f40b157006f734818] - I’m happy to answer.

Short answer is: *Yes,* you understood correctly, customers can use the funds from Bolt Balance only for services in Egypt via EG Partner.

Longer answer is:

* Let’s see it step by step:
** Customer is paying via inAPP card payment for the service, what EG Partner have served. Example: 100 EGP
*** Money is settled to EG Partner bank account (100 EGP minus payment fee’s)
** Customer is requesting the refund and agree it to add the money to Bolt Balance
*** Real Money is not moving (so, original payment is not going to refunded) → it stays there in EG Partner Bank account
*** Customer get in APP for Bolt Balance the same amount, what he wanted to refunded in local currency (so 100 EGP)
**** Customer can use the Bolt Balance only, when the same currency is available. (So, if we don’t have any other entities in EG, which use the same currency → everything is Super)
** Customer is ordering another service in EG market, which costs 250 EGP
*** System initiating the 150 EGP card payment and takes 100 EGP for Bolt Balance
*** Money is settled to EG Partner Bank account (150 EGP minus fees)
** If customer is going to Greece and ordering the service in EUR (customer can’t choose the currency)  and there are as well already refunded 100 EGP in Bolt Balance → Customer can’t use it.

So, we can say, that in EG → the Bolt Balance funds will be processed only trough EG Partner’s (not Bolt’s)

* Device Access: Multiple devices have accessed this rider's account. The starting point appears to be when this business client interacted with one of the drivers involved in the orders in early October. 
* Trip Patterns: The rider was pre-arranging trips with specific drivers. There are several trips conducted on the same day involving this passenger and the same drivers, suggesting some level of arrangement or agreement. Alternatively, this could indicate the account was already compromised and those trips were done by the imposter & his allies who accepted the trips. 

It's possible that the OTP was either shared with the driver or obtained illicitly. We know that since drivers have the passenger's phone number, they copy it and use it log into the rider's account ( on the rider app on their phones) before arriving at the pick-up location. Once arrived, they instruct the rider to share the OTP sent to be able to start the trip, and by so doing they gain access to the account and can even proceed to change the details.  

A detailed investigation into user relations, device relations, and implicated driver accounts will help rule out potential collusion or otherwise, and establish a clear timeline of events.

Hi [~accountid:615c8598a7071000699c8c93] and [~accountid:5f1a967bb8062200226b55c1] ☀️  Here are my answers, I also just finished with the ticket as well.

I used to focus on each element and the underlying root causes when I was writing my evaluation. I also used to be more detailed with each point in order to highlight agent issues. However, I would now focus on the general problem with potential action points after receiving great ticket-based feedback. I will also include more KB articles that are applicable to each situation and element that needs to be followed to. I will also avoid using a lot of acronyms.

# *Should I rate down Case Handling when the on-hold status was used multiple times for no reason or should I just leave a comment about it?*
Yes, we should rate down Case Handling when the on-hold status was used multiple times for no reason because we manage the cases according to Knowledge Base guidelines and we should follow the procedure. It could also imply that the assigned case was repeatedly left unresolved by multiple agents.
# *Where should I score down if the agent asked irrelevant questions that didn’t help the investigation?* 
We should rate down Relevant Information & Questions if the agent asked irrelevant questions that didn’t help the investigation.
# *We always aim to provide the best service, and that should be clear without saying it. But if I see sentences that don’t bring any value, then where should I mark it down and why?* 
We should score down Seamless Interaction because, it's important to be thoughtful and considerate, letting the customer know their concern is heard. Using that kind of sentence can also actually hurt trust and make customers doubt our honesty.
# *Can I rate the Empathy & Tone with thumbs up when the agent acknowledges the report by saying “Thank you for reaching out to us regarding this issue.“?*
Yes, we should rate Empathy & Tone down if the agent uses that kind of acknowledgment that looks very robotic, also “Regarding this issue” does not help recognise the user’s issue and can make them feel misunderstood/unacknowledged.
# *If I see the tool was logged on time, but the description of the events box was not filled in as per the KB guidelines, then what root cause do I need to select?*
'Incorrect tool information' root cause should be used in that case.

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *21 October 2024.*

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software. Hi Sandra,

From a Privacy POV, a disclaimer and T&Cs are indeed the main consideration here. In summary, we will need to do the following:

# Update the following template T&C to ensure it aligns with how this sweepstake is intended to work: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ybRlet8ae-IPsv5T7MemwjSEYiNGi0afYS5DQS3Nzb8/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ybRlet8ae-IPsv5T7MemwjSEYiNGi0afYS5DQS3Nzb8/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link] 
# Provide the user with a link to the T&C at the point they enter into the campaign, as part of some disclaimer wording.
# Ensure that we only retain email addresses specifically provided for this purpose for a limited period of time.

I include further details on these below.

*T&Cs*

For the sake of *_fairness_* and *_transparency_*, participants in this campaign should be able to understand how and on what conditions the prizes are assigned. ‘Random' allocation as a system is fine, provided that this is clearly explained. To ensure that we cover our bases in this regard, we recommend adapting our template ‘random giveaway’ T&C here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ybRlet8ae-IPsv5T7MemwjSEYiNGi0afYS5DQS3Nzb8/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ybRlet8ae-IPsv5T7MemwjSEYiNGi0afYS5DQS3Nzb8/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link]. Having these T&C in place also provides us with a legal basis for processing the participants’ personal data (i.e., their email address), and so further reduces privacy risks here.
Please note in particular Section 6.7 - we want to ensure that the data collected for this local campaign is not stored longer than needed - the standard approach is the duration of the campaign, but no longer than a few months.
Please therefore review the template and ensure the description of what data is collected and for what purposes is correct. I would then be happy to give it a final review.

*Disclaimer*

To ensure that the participants are able to access the T&C, as well as to further cover our bases from a transparency perspective, we should ensure that participants are provided with disclaimer wording at the point they enter the campaign.
* For new users, this would be when they fill out their email address after clicking the ad.
* For existing users, this would be in the lifecycle comms / email containing the promo code and informing them about the campaign.
The disclaimer wording should look something like this. The disclaimer refers the participant both to the relevant privacy notice and to the T&C:
“_By participating, your email address will be processed to determine and announce the winner, in line with GDPR Art. 6.1(b). It will be retained only as needed for this purpose._ {color:#4c9aff}+_Campaign T&Cs_+{color} _apply [_{color:#ff5630}_include hyperlink_{color}_]. For more on privacy and your rights, see our_ [+_Privacy Notice_+|https://bolt.eu/de-ch/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides].“

*Response to AKI in 1697-11 - audit trail on findings*:

* 👓  Glasses issue: AKI asked why did our system fail to detect glasses on the selfie if we instruct users to take them off → Glasses might affect face matching, that's why we instruct users to take them off. However it's not a hard requirement.
* 🛠️ Permanent solution to patch the vulnerability → We use "Request hashing" for prevening injected images. How it works: on Bolt App the image took by the user is sent to App store to generate a unique hash. This hash is received by the Backend servers, which run the image received on Backend through the same algorithm. If the same image is used, the resulting hash will be the same on the Backend as the one received from the App. Otherwise, if they differ, we conclude the image was injected.

The OTP was not physically *provided under duress by the actual driver (owner of the profile) but the perpetrators had access to it through the stolen device.* They had access which was granted through the authentication code provided by Bolt and not verbally provided by the driver. Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

# List of sub-processors is kept online. Therefore Bolt is not explicitly informed of the changes, i.e. Bolt would not give specific written authorization for the appointment of sub-processors.

# Notification of a data breach is set on 48 hours of becoming aware of the data breach.  Bolt would ideally require 24hrs generally for the mitigation of risk but we can approve 48hrs. 
# Bolt would be responsible for all costs and fees related to Supervisory Authority audit conducted of Bolt in regards to LinkedIn processing activities. 
# Upon request LinkedIn will provide a specific audit report conducted by third-party audit firm. For any additional audits Bolt would be responsible for all costs.

{{TL;DR}}
*We can enable Selfie-Verification, but it is risky and we may need to temporarily switch it off once Egypt's Executive Regulations are published, and the Data Protection Centre and its licensing regime are established. However, once we've obtained a license, we would be able to switch it back on.Biometric Data: Sensitive and Protected*
{panel}

* Selfie-verification relies on processing facial recognition biometric data, which Egypt classifies as *Sensitive Personal Data*.
* Processing this type of data triggers stricter compliance obligations and places additional scrutiny on how it is handled.

*Licensing and Consent Requirements*
To process biometric data like this, two key requirements under the PDPL must be addressed:

# *Licensing :* A license from Egypt’s Data Protection Center is mandatory for handling Sensitive Personal Data. However, here’s the catch—while the law is clear on the need for licensing, the government hasn’t issued the regulations needed to apply for one. This leaves us in a bit of a regulatory limbo, where the rules exist but the tools to comply with them do not.
# *Consent :* Explicit consent from users is required. We already obtain this when users choose to use automated selfie-verification with Bolt.

*The Risk of Non-Compliance*

* Considering that the Executive Regulations have not yet been published, we can't comply with the requirement to obtain a license (even if we wanted to). By switching Selfie-Verification on in Egypt, we are processing biometric data in non-compliance with the law in Egypt.
* There are both monetary penalties are imprisonment possibilities for non-compliance. Fines range from €14,500 to €145,000. Imprisonment could be up to three months for violations.
* However, the fact that Egypt's Data Protection Authority (the Data Protection Centre) is not yet established/operational does lower the risk somewhat - from high to *medium* .

Hey, I can answer your questions as that’s indeed related to an OPS/compliance task.

* {color:#0747a6}*What is the DVLA code?*{color}
** We use the UK GOV website to regularly check the validity of driver licences in the UK.  For the check to be performed, we are using details provided by the driver as part of the onboarding process and we enter them into the following UK GOV database [https://www.viewdrivingrecord.service.gov.uk/driving-record/licence-number|https://www.viewdrivingrecord.service.gov.uk/driving-record/licence-number|smart-link], which allows for checking driving licence status. The details we need for the check to be performed are:
*** the driver's license number
*** the national insurance number
*** the postcode of the driver’s address
** The check results in a DVLA licence summary (PDF document) which we store on the driver’s profile as evidence of the check being performed and its result.
* {color:#0747a6}*Have you checked the document allegedly uploaded by an unauthorized person? Does the document match his details?*{color}
** The document that the driver sees was uploaded by Bolt compliance agent after performing the check. We do this check on onboarding and then every 6 months to keep checking their entitlement to drive.
* {color:#0747a6}*Do we notice any new devices added to that account? Any other flags that might suggest that it was an unauthorized person that did so?*{color}
** No unauthorized access, this is done by Bolt’s compliance team as described above.

For{color:#0747a6} *further context*{color}, this has been set up based on the requirement imposed by TfL to verify driver details and documentation provided where possible (TfL Condition 10: The operator shall ensure that it has in place, and makes use of, appropriate checks to verify that all documentation provided by a driver is legitimate and that it relates to that driver. This will include, but is not limited to, *use of online tools such as* TfL Licence Checker, Daily Download reports, *the DVLA* and Home Office *websites* as well as direct contact with insurance companies). 


We are also removing drivers from the platform and informing TfL immediately if the check shows that the driver’s driving licence was disqualified, so TfL is very well aware of us performing these checks. 


We have these processes documented in detail on Confluence (I’m also sharing the screenshot of the main page here with the info on how it looks like, what details are needed and what details agents check) - let me know if you have any further questions.

We have received feedback from MaestroQA Legal team. Most of the comments were accepted and they have a few points to clarify.

* 8.3 - Termination for convenience
* 9.2 - Warranty language

+*UPDATE,  Laylas*+ {color:#ff5630}+*responses*+ {color}+*to Mike Roberts email.*+ 



+*(1) Intro / Recap*+

For the purposes of this note, please completely ignore any ability that Bolt has to rely on the Tour Operators Margin Scheme (TOMS) for tax purposes.

Under a principal model, an operator is going to be making chargeable supplies on the consideration paid for transportation services (i.e. the fare) which has VAT consequences.

A major risk we are trying to avoid at Bolt is moving to operating what we +truly+ consider to be an agency model but then we unexpectedly end up having to account for VAT on the chargeable supply of the fare, for 'some unforeseen reason'. This is the crux of all issues.

Recapping, the outcome from the London UTAG case (as then put into regulation under reg. 9(14) of the [Private Hire Vehicles (London) (Operators' Licences) Regulations 2000|https://content.tfl.gov.uk/phv-operator-licence-regulations-2000-consolidated-sept-2022.pdf] as amended) clearly stipulates a +_requirement_+ for operators to contract with passengers to 'provide the journey'. That effectively +_prohibits_+ Bolt operating under an agency model pursuant to its TfL licence. However re: Sefton, I'm mindful that we could end up in a similar situation even if the 'final outcome' does +_not_+ +_prohibit_+ an agency model: if it was possible to 'contractually operate an agency model' but 'still be treated (for tax purposes and otherwise) as principal' because of a 'deemed contract' this would be very significant to us.

+*(2) The deemed contract (ignoring 'purpose')*+ 

The following comments were made in the CoA judgment (at para. 22) - emphasis added:

_"The_ +_contract of hire_+ _must, in my judgment, refer to a contract under which_ +_the hirer_+ _agrees to give_ +_consideration_+ +_for their transport in a private hire vehicle_+_. That person may or may not be the person who made the booking. [...] Thus, in my judgment if a_ +_contract of hire_+ _is made after the booking is accepted (for instance when the driver arrives to pick up a passenger) that_ +_contract of hire_+ _is_ +_deemed_+ _to be made_ +_with the operator_+ _who accepted the booking."_

My reading of this is that the CoA thinks that the contract 'to be deemed' is:

* a contract for hire
* for the transport of a hirer in a private hire vehicle
* made for consideration
* with the operator

Q: In effect, ^+that+^ appears to be the contract that the CoA believes ought to be deemed, however Bolt decides to contractually operate. Ignoring the below point (2) on 'purpose', do you agree with this?

{color:#ff5630}I do not know the full details of the basis of the Bolt model on contracting, eg. it would require a scrutiny of the Terms and Conditions and also the basis of the driver being engaged (and I suspect the worker point would have a significant impact on this), however I agree with you on what is deemed and that the contract as deemed can be in existence in reality (i.e. if Bolt chooses to also operate on this basis) but may also not be in existence (i.e. in an agency model). The important wording of s56 is that it is only deemed “for the purpose of this Part of the Act” – i.e. for licencing under the 1976 Act.{color}

+*(3) The 'purpose' of the deemed contract*+

The CoA did go on to say as follows, which I acknowledge may materially dilute the impact of 'the deemed contract' (if held):

_"Fifth, the deeming provision applies for “_+_the purposes of this Part of this Act_+_”; in other words for the purposes of the regulatory scheme and not for any other purpose._ +_If section 56(1) were to require an operator to enter into a contract in the real world with the hirer, that contract would have an existence beyond the regulatory scheme and would thus go beyond the regulatory purpose_+_."_

^This seems to indicate that 'the deemed contract' does not actually exist in the real world, or it doesn't beyond the 'regulatory purpose' (whatever that is). 

Q: The combination of these things leads me to believe that Bolt's ability to be treated for tax purposes as if it was operating a 'true agency model' rests very heavily on what "for the purposes of this Part of this Act" actually means. Do you agree?

{color:#ff5630}Yes, I agree this is the key distinction.{color}

 The sort of risk I'm mindful of is, for example, if the Supreme Court decided that “for the purposes of this Part of this Act” did not have the limited impact suggested by the CoA. In that case, the deemed contract might be a 'very real world contract' between Bolt and passenger "for consideration" (as per the red text above) - arguably creating a taxable supply as if we +_were_+ operating a principal model, which would then be the case:

* whatever the contractual arrangements were between the parties;
* even if there was +*not*+ actually any +requirement+ to operate under a +principal model+;
* even if there was +*not*+ actually any +prohibition+ preventing operation under an +agency model.+

Q: As it stands, do you think a possible outcome re: Sefton might be that operators are 'deemed' to have contracts under which they make supplies for consideration, regardless of whether an agency model is prohibited or not?

 {color:#ff5630}If there was an extension of “For the purposes of this part of the Act” I think the second of your bullet points falls away, i.e. it is beyond deeming for only licensing and therefore it is imposing a contract for other purposes. The argument against this is that those words HAVE to mean something. Statutory  interpretation is about interpreting the words of parliament, that doesn’t allow us to ignore the words which are there whilst implying something else.{color}

{color:#ff5630}What Uber seek to argue is that what is deemed is actually required and is “for the avoidance of doubt”.{color}

{color:#ff5630}I think what you are suggesting is that the deemed contract is deemed (not for the avoidance of doubt) so can be in place of an actual contract with a driver but is for all purposes. I think for the reason above this is unlikely but of course it is possible. I don’t recall seeing this argued before the lower courts rather it is argued there must be a contract in reality for the purpose of public safety.{color}

 +*(4) The 'regulatory purpose' of the deemed contract*+

 I raise these issues in part as it's not very obvious to me how this 'deemed contract for hire' _could_ exist 'for regulatory purposes only'. The 'deemed contract' must be of some actionable consequence otherwise it would render s.56(1) pointless. At the same time, if the intention was simply to impose regulatory obligations onto the operator, then it would have just said so. I'm mindful that Uber might use that line of argumentation to try and collapse the CoA's analysis on this point (i.e. attempt to discredit it as a 'technical legal interpretation' that has no possible meaning).

 I'm also very mindful of the following comments (albeit obiter) in the UTAG case:

 _"31. Section 56 of the 1976 Act, set out above, supports [that a principal model is required]. It provides that every contract for the hire of a licensed private hire vehicle outside London shall be deemed to be made with the operator who accepted the booking for that vehicle whether or not he himself provided the vehicle. That demonstrates a clear parliamentary intention that the operator should undertake contractual responsibility. The language of the 1998 Act is different, but there is no reason for any different parliamentary intention in relation to private hire vehicle services in London."_

 Q: All things considered, is there any obvious way that this 'non-real world, for regulatory purposes only' contact might be readily said to be meaningful? Please do not spend long considering this, if nothing immediately comes to mind - the answer can just be 'not immediately known'.

{color:#ff5630} We have considered with counsel (including tax counsel) the issue about what is deemed, we diverge slightly but it is not significant for the tax purposes. It could mean it is required for whatever is required of an operator under the Act, that is mostly record keeping but could extend through licensing conditions. However, we conceded in the Court of Appeal a slightly wider interpretation, namely that this would enable a passenger to sue the operator under contract.{color}

{color:#ff5630}We consider the regulatory purpose cannot be extended to mean for tax purposes, and the guidance on PH from HMRC supports this (it refers to whether the driver is acting under agency model as the basis of who is providing the supply of service).{color}

{color:#ff5630}Tax counsel’s view is that a tax tribunal would look at the reality (not the deemed contract) in terms of who is making the supply. If I use the example of Delta they do not take any of the fare, that helps in identifying that it is the driver making the supply. This would not be the only question but the concept that the tax is related to the actual supply and not a deemed one is something which the HMRC guidance supports. The caselaw also supports that the issue is one of fact (and here you do get an overlap with TOMS) –{color}{color:#ff5630} +_HMRC -v- Secret Hotels 2 Limited [2014] UKSC 16._+{color}

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *22 October 2024.*



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 



As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software. Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail, we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.



We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Order History*



For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/|smart-link] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.



*Your rights* 



In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.





Yours sincerely,



Bolt

* Closing issues: When identifying issues with the closing block, use the correct and specific root cause. I had used an incorrect root cause under the Seamless interaction element for the lack of the closing block. When rating the building blocks, I would look at each block individually and ensure that the correct structure was followed e.g closing issues for a missing closing block
* Compensation actions issues: The process states that compensation is 50% of the final fare. I would look at the submitted compensation amount from the agent's POV as they would follow the documented process and not look at the actual issue with the final trip price, such as not ending the trip, as that is not part of the process.
* Automated comments do not count as backend actions. If the process requires a comment, then the comment would need to be added by the agent, regardless of the automated comment added by Alfred.
* N/A: This should only be used if that element is not required in the process. N/A should not be used if the agent added an additional internal note or backend action that was not necessary as per the process. In that case, the element should be rated down as the process was not followed.
* Empathy: While apologizing for the behavior of a rider or driver is not allowed, we can apologize for their experience. I would avoid rating agents down for expressing empathy for the experience that a user had on a trip.
* Feedback: When providing feedback, my comments were not specific to each element and did not provide actionable feedback and specific solutions. To avoid this, my comments will be separated into different elements. Each element will have an explanation of the error and also provide a specific and actionable expectation for the element, including possible examples and links to KB articles.  
* Automation: My initial error was not taking into account legacy interactions by Alfred. To avoid this, automation interactions, including legacy interactions will also be rated in the interaction.

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *14 October 2024.*



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 



As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software. Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail, we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.



We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you*  to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Invoices* 



For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/|https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/], which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.



*Your rights* 



In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

Yours sincerely,

*Update:* 


* DLA Piper tool - main points:
* The tool is an *Excel spreadsheet* with embedded mathematical algorithms.
* The tool assesses data transfers based on the following five criteria:
** Local data protection laws.
** Access to data by public authorities.
** The availability of redress mechanisms and the ease of exercising this right.
** The status and independence of the data protection authority.

# Investigate why CPU usage increased

*In Progress*

# Document findings:

h3. *Investigation Summary*

When Redis fails during chaos testing, all cache calls (both {{get}} and {{set}}) fail, triggering a fallback mechanism that retrieves data from the disk using {{toolset.getAllProvidersDetailsForH3CellAsBytes()}}. This fallback process is slower, disk I/O-intensive, and adds CPU overhead due to serialization and deserialization. The repeated failures also lead to excessive {{FireAndForget}} tasks, contributing to increased event loop lag, higher latency, and resource consumption.

----

h3. *Detailed Investigation*

During chaos testing  up to ~60K record count on average available in logs [https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r/s/bvYjB|https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r/s/bvYjB]

Compared to ~100 record count on average available in logs [https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r/s/4VGfL|https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r/s/4VGfL]

h4. *1. Redis Failures and Logs*

* Chaos testing fails all Redis operations ({{CHAOS_TESTING_ERROR(9970)}}).
* Highlighted Log Details:
** {{Log 1}} ({{Failed to get cache response for getProvidersWithMetadataFromCacheOrDisk}}) occurred 347,237 times.
** {{Log 2}} ({{Failed to set cache response for getProvidersWithMetadataFromCacheOrDisk}}) occurred 346,813 times.
** Both errors appear together almost always within the [analyzed time range|https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r/s/jycpS]: {{06/11/2024 11:14:41.000 - 06/11/2024 11:23:42.000}}
** In the code, the error messages come from [getProvidersWithMetadataFromCacheOrDisk|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/828ab230471b145f19f1a851c70a0faf6b1d8d7d/src/platform/geo/delivery_hex_cold_distance_matrix/main/service/DeliveryHexColdDistanceMatrixService.ts#L429-L484]

!image-20241119-073022.png|width=1913,height=1151,alt="image-20241119-073022.png"!

h4. *2. Fallback Mechanism*

* Code Behavior:
** When Redis fails, data is retrieved from the disk using [toolset.getAllProvidersDetailsForH3CellAsBytes()|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/828ab230471b145f19f1a851c70a0faf6b1d8d7d/src/platform/geo/delivery_hex_cold_distance_matrix/main/service/DeliveryHexColdDistanceMatrixService.ts#L458].
** The retrieved data is serialized ([toString("base64")|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/828ab230471b145f19f1a851c70a0faf6b1d8d7d/src/platform/geo/delivery_hex_cold_distance_matrix/main/service/DeliveryHexColdDistanceMatrixService.ts#L458]) and deserialized ({{Buffer.from()}}), increasing memory and CPU usage.
* Performance Impact:
** Disk operations are slower than cache retrieval, leading to a noticeable increase in latency.
** Disk I/O increases, as observed in the rise in IOPS during chaos testing.

h4. *3. Event Loop Lag*

* Metrics show a clear correlation between chaos testing and event loop lag spikes.
* The lag is a result of:
** High volume of [FireAndForget|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/828ab230471b145f19f1a851c70a0faf6b1d8d7d/src/platform/geo/delivery_hex_cold_distance_matrix/main/service/DeliveryHexColdDistanceMatrixService.ts#L464] retries.
** Additional CPU pressure from disk I/O and serialization overhead.

----

h3. Possible action items

* Optimize the Fallback Mechanism: batch disk reads If multiple fallback operations are triggered for the same data, batch them to reduce redundant disk I/O or perform serialization improvements evaluate if the current approach can be replaced with more efficient serialization methods.
* Enhance FireAndForget Task Handling: fail fast if Redis is confirmed down, skip {{FireAndForget}} tasks entirely to prevent wasted processing.

[~accountid:5dbb027ba766000da47cf09d] 

Before we take any decisions, has this issue been communicated to the driver? Since from the technical side the calculations are correct and Bolt has provided its services without defects, the matter is actually between the driver and the rider. However, I understand we don’t want to just forward the rider’s complaint to the driver and leave it at that – that doesn’t create a good customer experience for either side. In any case, I believe we should get the driver’s thoughts on the issue (simply as part of our due diligence, if nothing more).

Having said that, it likely that the rider is essentially right, however the cited sections of the law are not entirely correct. The second paragraph of section 6 of the Consumer Services Act (SFS 1985:716) states that:

“_If it becomes apparent only after work has commenced that the service cannot be regarded as being of reasonable benefit to the consumer,_ +_or that the price of the service may be appreciably higher than the consumer could have expected_+_, the undertaking shall advise the consumer of the situation and request further instructions_.”

This means that the rider should have been informed of the price increase during the ride and as soon as the price increase was apparent. Legally, this obligation falls on the driver (or the fleet) as they are the one providing the transportation service. However, since it is our platform and our tools that affect this whole relationship, it possible that there is also an error on our part.

Before giving a final assessment on the matter, I would like to clarify a few things:

# Was the original accepted price a +fixed price+ or an +estimation+? If an estimation, then how is the price communicated to the rider via the app interface – i.e., is it clear that the price shown at the start is an estimation? And are they made aware of how the fare is calculated?
# Can we make an assumption as to when was it apparent that the price would be significantly higher – did this happen sometime during the ride or at the very end?
# Do we have in place any sort of notification functionality for when a high price increase becomes apparent? If not, was the driver generally able to see that the price increased during the ride?
## If yes, then we may argue that since it was the driver’s obligation to notify the rider and we have done reasonable efforts to enable the driver to see this info, then the rider is likely entitled to a refund of the price increase on behalf of the driver (unless the driver had reason to expect that we would notify the rider on their behalf).
## If not, then this would be an error on our part. It is difficult to fault the driver for not complying with the law if it was impossible or difficult because of the tools provided by us (i.e., the platform). In such a case we should consider refunding the rider the price increase and take the loss ourselves, or alternatively ask if the rider would be OK with getting a discount code for the same value.

* Another suggestion to reduce the number of JOINs is to avoid joining the same table multiple times. The current approach filters data in the {{reusable_authorisation}} table by joining the {{booking_item}} table twice:  
{noformat}SELECT
  /*+ MAX_EXECUTION_TIME(7866) */
  initial_booking_item.booking_id AS initial_booking_id
FROM
  reusable_authorisation t
  JOIN booking_item initial_booking_item ON initial_booking_item.id = t.initial_booking_item_id
  JOIN booking_item target_booking_item ON target_booking_item.id = t.target_booking_item_id
WHERE
  t.user_id = 120365034
  AND t.user_type = 'user'
  AND t.state = 'reused'
  AND target_booking_item.booking_id = 2378626844
ORDER BY
  t.created DESC
LIMIT
  1{noformat}
Instead, you can simplify the filter condition by using an AND clause in the WHERE condition, as shown below:  
{noformat}SELECT
  bt.booking_id AS initial_booking_id
FROM reusable_authorisation t USE INDEX(reusable_authorisation_user_id_state_user_type_idx)
  JOIN booking_item bt ON bt.id = t.initial_booking_item_id
WHERE t.user_id   = 139165070
  AND t.user_type = 'user'
  AND t.state     = 'reused'
  AND t.target_booking_item_id IS NOT NULL
  AND bt.booking_id = 2378577196
  AND bt.id         = t.target_booking_item_id
ORDER BY
  t.created DESC
LIMIT 1{noformat}

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *4 November 2024.*



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 



As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software. Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail, we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.



We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Order History* 



For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/|smart-link] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.



*Your rights* 



In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.





Yours sincerely,



Bolt

We are generating payouts directly to the courier rather than the fleet because their balance is incorrectly linked to their personal profile instead of the fleet’s profile.

The issue likely stems from an incorrect setup during registration, where the courier was mistakenly set up as an individual courier instead of as part of the fleet.

*Solution:*
To resolve this, the courier’s balance must be transferred to the fleet’s balance to ensure payouts go to the fleet.

*Important Note:*
While we now understand the problem and required action, it’s important to note that Billing is unable to transfer the courier’s balance to the fleet’s balance directly.

*Next Steps:*
CY local operations (as well as all global local operations) are required to manually adjust balances themselves using [this|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/3717988516/Manual+Adjustments+New+Process+Guides?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiNTEyZjljZDdhMmJkNDBiNWI3YWM0ZTM5OGQxY2VkNTEiLCJwIjoiY29uZmx1ZW5jZS1jaGF0cy1pbnQifQ] guide.

Passkey authentication is not available on driver app, none of our security assumptions for authentication hold if device is stolen. Best thing user can do is enable fingerprint/faceID for their phone as it protects all of their apps. 

Yet as phone is not locked during the ride, it would still be possible for the robber to get access to it and thus bypass these protections (or even force victim to disclose password under threat of force).

_When we provide Health & Benefits insurance broking services, like we do for BOLT,  we undertake these processing activities in the role of independent Data Controller. We act as Data Controller because we determine the purposes and means of the processing of the personal information you share with us. This means that we determine what to do with such personal information and why (purposes) and how exactly to do it (means).  For the purposes of the law, the moment we begin making decisions on the purposes and means of the processing we are classed as a Data Controller. For example, we make decisions regarding the following:_

* _Whether to collect the personal information in the first place;_
* _Which categories of information to collect (i.e., what should be the content);_
* _Which individuals to collect the information about;_
* _How to use the information (e.g., provision of services, marketing, profiling, R&D, Customer Relationship Management (CRM), compliance, etc.);_

* _What software or hardware to use to process the information;_
* _How (e.g., paper or electronic), where and for how long to retain the information, and when to delete it; or_
* _Whether to transfer the data cross border_

_As such, the position that we are Data Controllers is based on a factual assessment.
