Further, both WTW Nigeria and WTW Ghana have provided Bolt with their respective General Terms Of Business Agreement For Health & Benefits Clients which detail how WTW will treat and protect information shared with WTW at all times in accordance with the applicable data protection legislation. Further, if you require further information on how WTW handles privacy matters, please refer to WTW’s Global Privacy Notice which can be accessed via this link_ [https://www.wtwco.com/en-gb/notices/global-website-privacy-notice|https://www.wtwco.com/en-gb/notices/global-website-privacy-notice|smart-link]

Hey Iiris! 

Let’s imagine the following scenarios: 

*Scenario 1: A passenger refuses to leave the car. Does this restrict the driver’s movement?*
Yes, because:
a. If the driver starts driving the car, it could be considered as kidnapping, even if they intend to transport the passenger to a police station.
b. While the driver could technically exit the car with the passenger still inside, this action poses a risk due to the unpredictability of the passenger’s behavior.

*Scenario 2: A group of passengers surrounds the car. Does this restrict the driver’s movement?*
Yes, because:
a. The driver cannot drive away without risking harm to the passengers, which could result in running them over.
b. Although the driver could technically leave the car, doing so also puts them at risk due to the unpredictable behavior of the group.

*Scenario 3: (the one you described) The passenger somehow locks the driver inside the car. Does this restrict the driver’s movement?* 

Yes, but

a. If the driver is unable to leave, this means that most likely the passenger stole the car keys. Such cases will be taken with a different EC.

----

 The above-mentioned scenarios (1 and 2) were taken from a case deep-dive that I did for cases taken as Rider Unlawfully Detained The Driver; these 2 cases were the most common reasons (and the only ones) for this EC. The scenario for the rider locking up the driver in the car must be taken with a different EC as the main one.

If you have better suggestions on what ECs to apply for the cases described above (scenarios 1 and 2), please let me know 🙂 

Galina

Hi [~accountid:5f01e8651c682d0029d6ea82] 

Bolt contributes up to 50% cost of the Essential Delta Saver plan. On the Classic Delta Saver plan (which is a higher plan than the EssDelta Saver) you will only get an employer contribution of up to 50% cost of the EssDelta Saver and you pay the difference.

*Example:* If the cost of the EssDelta Saver was R3,000 - Bolt would contribute R1,500 _(50% cost of the EssDelta saver)_ towards the medical aid premium of an employee who elects to be on the EssDelta Saver or higher plan. What this means is that if the Classic Delta Saver plan, being a higher plan to the EssDelta Saver, cost R4,000 the employee would be liable for more than 50% cost of the chosen plan i.e. you would hypothetically speaking pay R2,500 and Bolt pays R1,500 *_(which is 50% cost of the EssDelta Saver plan)_*_._

Electing the Essential Delta Saver or lower plan places you at an advantage to get a full 50% employer contribution, meaning there would be an even split between what you’d pay and what Bolt pays towards your medical aid cover.

Makes sense? If not, set up a 15 mins call with me sometime.

Heuristically here is the query I found to get us what we want. Maybe there are more processes updating issues though, but TBC, the business output should be similar to this query:

{code:sql}WITH issue_update AS (
    SELECT
        se.id, 
        se.support_case_id, 
        se.event_type, 
        NULLIF(se.issue_keys_added,'[]') AS agent_added_issues, 
        NULLIF(se.issue_keys_removed,'[]') AS agent_removed_issues,
        NULLIF(get_json_object(se.event_data, '$.reported_issues'),'[]') AS entry_point_added_issues,
        NULLIF(get_json_object(se.event_data, '$.new_issue_keys'),'[]') AS model_added_issues,
        si.interaction_reply_selected_option AS user_added_issues
    FROM ng_customer_support_spark.support_case_event se
    LEFT JOIN core_models_spark.fact_support_case_interaction si
      ON si.interaction_request_event_id = se.id
        AND si.interaction_type = 'issue_key_selection_automation'
        AND si.support_case_created_date_utc >= DATE('2024-11-01')
    LEFT JOIN core_models_spark.fact_support_case sc
      ON sc.support_case_id = se.support_case_id
    WHERE se.created_date >= DATE('2024-11-01')
        AND sc.support_case_created_date_utc >= DATE('2024-11-01')
        AND sc.is_incoming_support_case is TRUE
        AND sc.support_case_state = 'closed'
        AND (
          NULLIF(se.issue_keys_added,'[]') IS NOT NULL OR
          NULLIF(se.issue_keys_removed, '[]') IS NOT NULL OR
          NULLIF(get_json_object(se.event_data, '$.reported_issues'),'[]') IS NOT NULL OR
          NULLIF(get_json_object(se.event_data, '$.new_issue_keys'),'[]') IS NOT NULL OR
          si.interaction_reply_selected_option IS NOT NULL
        )
    ORDER BY se.id
)
SELECT
  sc.support_case_id,
  COALESCE(iu.id, 1) AS event_id, 
  CASE
    WHEN iu.agent_added_issues IS NOT NULL AND iu.agent_removed_issues IS NOT NULL THEN 'agent_issues_updated'
    WHEN iu.agent_added_issues IS NOT NULL THEN 'agent_issues_added'
    WHEN iu.agent_removed_issues IS NOT NULL THEN 'agent_issues_removed'
    WHEN iu.entry_point_added_issues IS NOT NULL THEN 'entry_point_issues_added'
    WHEN iu.model_added_issues IS NOT NULL THEN 'model_issues_added'
    WHEN iu.user_added_issues IS NOT NULL THEN 'user_issues_added'
    WHEN iu.support_case_id IS NULL THEN 'no_issues_event'
    ELSE 'agent_issues_added'
  END AS update_process, 
  row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY sc.support_case_id  ORDER BY iu.id) AS rank,
  COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY sc.support_case_id) AS count_issue_update_event
FROM core_models_spark.fact_support_case sc
LEFT JOIN issue_update iu
  ON sc.support_case_id = iu.support_case_id
WHERE sc.support_case_created_date_utc >= DATE('2024-11-01')
  AND sc.is_incoming_support_case is TRUE
  AND sc.support_case_state = 'closed'{code}

{quote}The Partner has signed the Agreement for use of Bolt Food Platform for Partner that states that the Agreement is comprised of both the Special Terms and the General Terms. The Partner is subject to our General Terms available here: [https://bolt.eu/ro-ro/legal/tnc-bolt-food-partner/?category=delivery.|https://bolt.eu/ro-ro/legal/tnc-bolt-food-partner/?category=delivery.|smart-link] 

According to the General Terms Bolt has the following rights:

# Bolt has the right to amend the Agency Fee by providing the Partner a prior written notice at least 30 days in advance (clause 6.2 of the General Terms).
# Bolt has the right to send notices related to the Agreement via email (clause 13.4 of the General Terms).
# Bolt has the right to update the General Terms anytime by uploading the updated version on its website and by notifying the Partner of the changes at least 30 days in advance (clause 13.6 of the General Terms).

Therefore, Bolt acted in accordance with the terms of the agreement concluded between Bolt and the Partner.{quote}

However, there is one weak point in this line of argument. Clause 13.4 of the General Terms that allows Bolt to send notices and communication by email mentions that there should be proof of receipt. Since as you mentioned we have now changed the system we will not be able to show the proof of receipt. This is a valid point that the Partner can raise, however, they have been paying the updated Agency Fee for a year and it is also reasonable for Bolt to argue that this constituted a valid acceptance of the new Agency Fee. Both parties are required to act in a good faith and party claiming to have suffered a loss is under the obligation to minimise its losses, however, it does not look like the Partner took reasonable steps and conducted a timely review of the financials of its business therefore the Partner did not take sufficient steps to minimise its loss.

As to other partners - all of them (except some key accounts) are subject to our General Terms and the same reasoning can be applied when we amend the Agency Fee. However, there are some Partners that requested to eliminate Bolt’s right to amend the Agency Fee unilaterally in the Special Terms, so you need to check if the Special Terms specifically prohibit Bolt from amending Agency Fee without Partner’s consent.

The only material outstanding items are the Indemnification and Limitation of Liability and we've proposed solution's that hopefully will be acceptable. 

* +Indemnification+: 

** The point under discussion is whether or not Brighthire should indemnify Bolt if it has been abiding by the terms of the DPA _and_ it still suffers or causes a personal data breach.  
** Under GDPR, Controllers are responsible for personal data security and for ensuring that all of their processors are implementing appropriate technical and organization security measures.  
** Also under GDPR (Art 82), Controllers and Processors are each liable to data subjects for personal data breaches and can claim back from each other the part of the compensation corresponding to their part of the responsibility for the data
** Given these two facts, our perspective is that Brighthire should not contractually have to indemnify Bolt under these circumstance.
** That said, we added language to make it clear that we would be liable to Bolt under Art 82.  
* +Limitation of Liability+

** As I believe we've mentioned, our Board will not let us enter into contracts with uncapped internal liabilities.
** We had proposed a cap of $3m and you all had countered with $5m per claim.
** We can accept a total of $5m but not $5m per claim.  

If these changes are acceptable to Aleksander, I think we can finalize the document quickly async. Hello Debora,

Thank you for your thoughtful and detailed response.

Before proceeding further, I would like to reiterate some critical points outlined in the business case attached to the ticket, as they directly impact the feasibility of this agreement with Banca Transilvania.

# *The Liability Clause is Non-Negotiable for the Client*

During our initial discussions, I made an effort to explain our current stance on liability and provided reasoning similar to what you outlined in your response. However, the client emphasized that this clause is non-negotiable due to their unique regulatory environment.

As Romania’s largest banking institution, Banca Transilvania is subject to intense regulatory scrutiny. Their primary concerns stem from strict Romanian laws governing labor safety, commercial obligations, and criminal liability.

* *Labor Law:* Romanian labor regulations impose severe penalties (linked to company revenue) for safety-related infractions affecting employees.
* *Commercial Law:* The lack of provider accountability in a contract could be flagged as a compliance risk by auditors or authorities.
* *Criminal Law:* Romanian law does not allow the limitation of criminal liability through contractual terms, making a blanket exclusion of liability unfeasible in this context.

# *Proposed Workaround*

The rephrased liability clause suggested in the ticket aims to address these concerns while maintaining a reasonable level of protection for Bolt. It specifies liability only in instances where third-party providers fail to meet the express compliance and documentation standards required by Bolt’s platform. This limitation ensures that:

* Bolt remains protected from undue liability.
* The clause aligns with our platform’s regulatory structure and operational safeguards.
* It satisfies the client’s need for accountability, avoiding significant legal and reputational risks on their end.

# *Strategic Importance of the Client*

Banca Transilvania represents a high-value client, not just in terms of GMV (€1,176,000 annually) but also as a key strategic partner and logo acquisition. Securing this agreement could unlock opportunities within their ecosystem and open doors to other financial institutions in Romania and beyond.

Given these factors, I believe that exploring the proposed rephrasing of the liability clause could provide a viable path forward, balancing the client’s regulatory needs with Bolt’s risk tolerance.

Please let me know your thoughts on this approach or if you see alternative solutions that align with both legal and business priorities.

Thank you for your continued support, and I look forward to your guidance.

🚨 IMPORTANT:

[~accountid:60bd1ba4a17463007037063d] noticed an important change between IOT FW 2102 and 2305, and decided to investigate the frequency of updating battery SOC.

Our system considers the latest battery SOC update to calculate the % drop / km. The SOC (battery %) is reported direcly by the IOT, and the logic of reading the battery voltage to translate to SOC is unknown. These are the behaviors of both IOT FWs:

* FW 2102 seems to update battery SOC very rarely or at random times (i.e. once per 4-5 minutes). This often leads to the battery SOC status update a few minutes after the order ends. In this case, the system will consider the previous battery SOC status update before the order ended, usually while the ride was still active. As most of our rides have a short duration period (minutes) this lag between updates can cause our system to consider the incorrect battery SOC for creating the % drop / km report, reporting a lower consumption than reality. In [this example|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-micromobility/vehicles/iot/view/585786?tab=logs&filter=%7B%22offset%22%3Anull%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22lines%22%3A100%2C%22from_ts%22%3A1731053815%2C%22to_ts%22%3A1731054720%7D%7D], it takes almost 5 minutes to update the SOC, and then suddenly it drops by 4% when updates:
** 8:19:13 - 94%
** 8:24:02 - 94%
** 8:24:17 - 90%
* On FW 2305 the update rate seems to have increased to something like 30 seconds, due to the implementation of more detailed telemetry. In this case, the battery SOC report is more likely to happen closer to the end of the ride, minimizing the differences. One example [here|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-micromobility/vehicles/iot/view/582618?tab=logs&filter=%7B%22filter%22%3A%7B%22from_ts%22%3A1731054170%2C%22to_ts%22%3A1731054956%7D%7D].

To prove this theory, an analysis of rides in Zurich was conducted comparing the last battery SOC reported by the IOT before the end of the ride considered for the % drop/km report (iot_drop_per_km), and the adjusted lower battery SOC after the time the ride was finished:

# IOT FW 2102: 1659 out of 2245 orders (74%) show differences between what IOT reports as %drop/km and what was reported on the next update after the ride was finished.
# IOT FW 2305: 307 out of 3123 orders (9.8%) show differences between what IOT reports as %drop/km and what was reported on the next update after the ride was finished.

Analysis: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IO30KY-oCy9AxydnBlv2bx1LdMfxXgu2YasdBJWAi_E/edit?gid=1477980755#gid=1477980755|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IO30KY-oCy9AxydnBlv2bx1LdMfxXgu2YasdBJWAi_E/edit?gid=1477980755#gid=1477980755|smart-link] (Tab *_Zurich/2102/39 orders_* and *_Zurich/2305/39 orders_*)

We conclude the frequency of IOT battery SOC updates in FW 2102 led us to believe in the data provided through the battery % drop/km report, which is inaccurate for FW 2102, and way more precise for FW 2305.

To finally confirm our findings, we also looked into km-s between swaps for the two major systems Berlin and Stockholm, and we did not notice any difference during these last three years of operations, other than small fluctuations most likely caused by temperature or other external factors that not IOT FW. The assumption is that if the 50% increase in battery consumption happened, we would see big differences here, which we do not:

!Screenshot 2024-11-19 at 15.46.34.png|width=1527,height=765,alt="Screenshot 2024-11-19 at 15.46.34.png"!

!Screenshot 2024-11-19 at 14.38.13.png|width=1527,height=765,alt="Screenshot 2024-11-19 at 14.38.13.png"!

Therefore, our conclusion is that the low frequency of the battery SOC report and how our backend handles the data for this specific % drop/km led us to a wrong conclusion about battery consumption increase and that FW 2305 fixed this issue with a higher frequency SOP update.

Moving forward, we recommend first proceeding with the global ECU FW 3F update, which is proven to have a real impact on our business and operations, then followed by the IOT FW 2305 update to regain all the telemetry functions, also eliminating the need for handling different IOT HW versions in cities with Loc-ID in place.

analysis was done by looking at data from August/2024.

I’ve pulled every in-app order that didn’t have preauth. main metric will be from the columns:

* *max_risk_cost*: the assumption is that if an order had an initial failed payment, the user could run into the same error in the preauth that could cause the order not to be created. _max_risk_cost_ tracks the worst possible scenario where every single order that matches this criteria ends up not being created. loss to us is the order GMV vs Rides 8% profitability.
* *min_savings_same_price*: this column represents our main saving. if the order’s final price remains equal to or smaller than the amount we have authorized and is currently uncovered, then the payment won’t fail anymore.

*max_risk_cost* isn’t realistic. users should be able to change payment methods or top-up their cards to still create orders.

on the other end, *min_savings_same_price* is a guaranteed win.

therefore, if (*min_savings_same_price* - *max_risk_cost*) is positive, the outcome should be positive for Bolt.

the tab *_simplified numbers on the country level_* on the following sheet has country numbers: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/18v_OnyknnNbaIIj3dDIbn18zSd5F8h5328-QX5bvICk/edit?gid=0#gid=0|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/18v_OnyknnNbaIIj3dDIbn18zSd5F8h5328-QX5bvICk/edit?gid=0#gid=0|smart-link]

for some countries, if we start doing preauth for literally every single in-app order, the outcome should be positive. TH for example, has a *max_risk_cost* of 5.4k euros and *min_savings_same_price* of 10.1k euros. we would reduce 10.1k euros in failed payments risking at max 5.4k euros of net good GMV.

According to the TVDE law, our t&c must be aligned with the national legislation on general terms and conditions (namely [DL 446/85|https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/decreto-lei/446-1985-177869]). This legislation determines an obligation of communication and information, that in my opinion recommend that we aim at better communicating and informing TVDE operators of Bolt’s cleaning fee policy, namely in terms of acceptable documents. Having this in mind, we intend in the next revision of the t&c for TVDE operators to introduce an additional clause with the following language:

_“7.4. The cleaning fee referred to in clause 7.3. shall not exceed €120.00 (one hundred and twenty euros) and is subject to the presentation of evidence by the TVDE Operator and/or Driver, as well as review by Bolt. The TVDE Operator and/or Driver recognise that the cleaning fee is subject to these requirements. For more details, see_ [+_here_+|https://bolt.eu/en-pt/support/articles/4404972195858/]_.”_

It is important that requirements, such as not accepting recibos verdes, to be clearly mentioned in the FAQ where we provide details on this matter. # There are no specific EU or German regulations that prohibit this. # Additional requirements would apply if the speed limiter would be a “hard” limiter (i.e., no leeway), such as that installation can only be done by manufacturers of the vehicle or the speed limiter. However, these requirements do not apply to the Bolt speed limiter since it is a “soft” speed limiter (it is +35 km/h).
# Since all "new" EU vehicles will be required to have a speed limiter anyways, then having two speed limiters at the same time may cause issues for product safety. The suggestion is that if a car already has a speed limiter installed by the manufacturer, then Bolt speed limiter would be unnecessary – this should be taken into account when handling new cars.

* *Cash-blocking thresholds*: Defines the cash ride limits for blocking/unblocking cash rides for a driver. ** Minimal balance to unblock cash rides: The balance threshold where we will once again unblock the driver’s cash rides.

*Summary of the project (provided by the reporter):*

Commerce team has made a huge bet on the company Silverflow to integrate Bolt to the cards schemes (Visa and Mastercard) directly (cutting out processors like ProcessOut and Adyen).

After going fully live with Silverflow, we intend to direct 90% of EU and UK card traffic to that path reducing processing costs approximately 3M€ per year. We do not hold a card acquiring license however.

So for us to connect to card schemes directly, we also need "Sponsorship" (processing under someone elses license). And this is where Deutsche Bank comes in. They provide the sponsorship and the settlement money movements ("business connectivity"). Silverflow is who processes the transactions for us (technical connectivity).

*Request from business:*

To sign the Deutche Bank (DB) trial agreements with Bolt Operations OÜ and Bolt Services UK Ltd ([JIRA TICKET|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-42008]) ASAP as they want to start with testing with the existing documentation of DB, with negotiation on the documentation taking place during the testing phase.

* We will ONLY use Bolt payment team employee cards in this live trial. Not even all employees.
* We will only be allowed to do max 10 transactions per day.

Why this is urgent for business: the sooner we switch over, the sooner we can start saving around 285k€ / month for Bolt.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Summary of DB provided documentation:*

# There are no substantial provisions/agreements governing personal data transfer between DB and Bolt in the documents shared. Clause 17 in the Special Terms is not enough, and will only suffice to explain how DB processes personal data of Bolt`s employees/representatives in contract negotiations.
# At the present moment, Bolt lacks:
## a clear description of how Bank, Merchant (Bolt), and 3rd party payment scheme (Silverflow) will transfer personal data (credit card details, etc) between each other. Note that making available this data also amounts to transfer.
## a clear division of responsibilities based on the specific service that we are contracting (acquiring services).
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#ffebe6}
*Risks:*

It is difficult to estimate the risks of proceeding with DB without addressing points 1 and 2, as I do not fully understand how much data DB will actually have access to.

In theory, as a large commercial bank in the EU, we will likely face limited regulatory risks due to their obligations to maintain strong privacy compliance. However, proceeding without clarity on points 1 and 2 will put in question our compliance as we need to have a clear audit trail and clear documentation with suppliers.
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Privacy's advice (shared with the reporter in Slack):*

Privacy cannot endorse going forward with DB based on their standard privacy provisions, even considering that only Bolt employees data is involved for testing. It is your business decision to go against privacy/legal advice, if you believe going forward with the trial is important from business perspective and outweighs the risks.

To outline the risks from the privacy side: they are low-medium as I see them now;

# Probability of legal and regulatory risk (due to data breach/etc) is low, considering good reputation and regulatory supervision for DB & limited scope of processing during the test;
# Impact can be medium, as having no clear description and procedures for cooperation can result in ineffective response to incidents and data breaches, inquiries from our employees if they get interest in how their data processed in the test; etc - which ultimately may lead to breach of privacy laws.

Following the receipt of the advice, the reporter confirmed that Bolt decided to proceed with the trial agreement as is. Bolt and DB will negotiate privacy safeguards after the trial is completed if we decide to go forward with DB.
{panel}

*Family Accounts - Initial Privacy assessment.*

I have reviewed the following documents:

* [https://docs.google.com/document/d/131Unh-SZahuPgYLGGvXXo0CuiwbP8mCmYQ9tFOwyr7M/edit?tab=t.9isq0y709vrm|https://docs.google.com/document/d/131Unh-SZahuPgYLGGvXXo0CuiwbP8mCmYQ9tFOwyr7M/edit?tab=t.9isq0y709vrm|smart-link] 
* [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1aArEuyBeSbaIfTLu-wsMUPcxzK9exivYoj80ihkc_Nc/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1aArEuyBeSbaIfTLu-wsMUPcxzK9exivYoj80ihkc_Nc/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link] 

----

*Main points from a privacy standpoint:*

I see that essentially a Family account is about: 1) a shared payment method + management of spending limits and 2) viewing the members' activity (owner sees what members do, members see limited info on other members).

* Shared payment method is not something that’s problematic from privacy side; 
* viewing other members' activity is also allowed, however, we need to be very transparent and make it clear to the user about who can see what (see below).
** Regarding trip sharing/tracking - this part seems very close to the Trusted Contacts/Trip sharing features, so we don’t have any objections to this from a privacy standpoint.
* The most problematic part about Family Accounts is the use of children data. 



*Transparency*

* One of the pain points from a privacy POV is transparency. In short, we need to inform the users when, how, for what purposes and with whom we share their data. 
* We will need to be very clear when communicating this in-app, including with the invitations to join a family account. Members will have to be aware that other members/account owner will see what they’re doing. I’d like to ask to be looped into the review of the copies when we reach that stage.
** Note - banners / information needs to be provided for both the owner of the Family account and the members.
* We will have to update our privacy notice to reflect that we’re using personal data for this purpose. This task sits with the Privacy team, and we’d like to ask you to provide more information on the ETA for launch. 



*Use of Children data*

Using children’s data under GDPR poses significant challenges due to stricter requirements for obtaining valid consent when offering services directly to children under 16 (or lower, depending on the Member State, but not below 13 - differs per country). Key points:

# If a child is under the applicable age threshold, consent must be obtained or authorized by the holder of parental responsibility. In other words, for these children, we’ll need to obtain some form of parental consent on behalf of the child.
# We must make reasonable efforts to verify that consent is valid and given by the parent/guardian, considering the technology available. This means that we’d need to verify that the person giving consent is a parent/guardian.
# Failure to meet these requirements could result in non-compliance with GDPR, particularly where robust mechanisms to obtain and verify parental consent are lacking.

Therefore, I strongly advise to *exclude children from the use of this feature;* or, alternatively, *we need to come up with a parental consent solution.* 

*I suggest explicitly stating that a person needs to be over 18 to use this feature / to be added to the Family Account.* 



*Account security*

Recent phishing attacks, and other types of data incidents (e.g. recycled phone number incidents) show that we have certain gaps in our account safety. Since with this feature we are introducing the ability for a number of people to use another person’s payment method, I strongly advise you to thing about ways of making these accounts secure, for example, by introducing verification.



----

In addition, the difference in the amount would be more €600 and the total credit would be around €1,000. Given that Bolt is a creditor “comum“ Bolt (among others) is the last to receive the product of the sales of the insolvent, and sometimes these creditors do not receive any amount.

In view of the cost-benefit of this situation (lawyer fees + considering the low probability of recovering the credit and also the value of the credit at stake), we will not present a claim to the court.

After discussing this with the other component owners and with Siarhei in Slack DM, we’ve decided not to proceed with this feature due to the following concerns:

# *Risk of Misconfiguration:*
Allowing configurable dropping of events could lead to accidental misconfiguration, causing critical messages to be dropped unintentionally. This could result in production issues or loss of important data.
# *Complexity and Lack of Safety:*
Providing a safe, flexible, and testable configuration mechanism (e.g., via JSON or similar) is challenging. Such an approach could be error-prone and difficult to validate, especially under edge cases.

Additionally, we believe the same objectives can be achieved through component tests, which allow such scenarios to be simulated in a safer and more controlled environment.

Based on these considerations, we’ll reject this ticket.

        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'adherence_percentage' THEN hr.value END) AS adherence_percentage,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'actual_utilization_all_channels' THEN hr.value END) AS utilization_actual_all,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'in_office_shrinkage' THEN hr.value END) AS in_office_shrinkage,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'seconds_in_adherence' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_in_adherence,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'actual_seconds_in_adherence_bpo' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_in_adherence_actual_bpo
    from ng_fivetran_cs_assembled.hourly_report_metric hr
    join ng_fivetran_cs_assembled.people p
        on hr.agent_id = p.agent_id
    where hr.type = 'interval'
    group by p.email, from_unixtime(hr.start_time), from_unixtime(hr.end_time)
)


select * from base
limit 100;{noformat}
* Based on result, here are the formulas for main metrics:
** utilization_actual = seconds_worked / seconds_scheduled_total
** utilization_planned = seconds_scheduled_productive / seconds_scheduled_total
** conformance = seconds_worked / seconds_scheduled_productive
** adherence_percentage = seconds_in_adherence / seconds_scheduled_productive

# *The Driver reported that his phone number was changed in the app. If and when was the phone number changed in the Driver account?*
_The number was changed on 14th Nov by the driver himself meaning he had to have the old phone number available to confirm the change by SMS code. Then per fleet request by local OPS changed back to the original on 18th Nov, however, the real driver was available on this number._ 
# *Was it a fraudster who took over the real Driver’s account? What was the root cause, i.e. how did this happen?*
_As far as we know yes, when we called the driver via the profile set number he didn’t know a thing about an incident that has been discussed in the app and informed us his account has been misused for a few days already. In this chat in the app the person communicating with us (about the safety incident) requested us to call him on a different number (which was an immediate red flag) that is set in the app, per my advice the OS agent did call and by that confirmed it was a completely different person that the first one on call via profile set number. Agents took verification steps per KB in both calls and the person who was communicating with us in the app and was called on this requested number wasn’t able to pass verification, the driver (as we assume he is) called on the phone number in the app did pass the verification._
# *When did the misuse of the account begin?*
_We do not know for sure, driver reported misuse via verified email on 17th Nov here:_ [_https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/473864641_|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/473864641]
# *Current status of the Driver’s account. Does the Driver have control over his account now?*
_I requested ID verification with paper with current date in the email above, he did send us the document and has been further advised per KB to change password. As he then sent us screenshots from the app we can assume he did changed the password as otherwise he couldn’t access the account. Now this ticket was probably created by agents to confirm they can unblock the account._ 
# *Did the Driver suffer any harm (i.e. financial, money withdrawn from their account etc.)?*
_Inconclusive, payout is only being sent to fleet so quite the opposite, any earnings made by this fraudster (apart from cash ones) will be paid to the driver’s fleet and to the driver. However, this may indicate the misuse by someone in the fleet but that is not up to us to investigate._ 
# *Were there any other account details changed?*
_No._

However, this doesn’t mean that we should not work with hotels as there are potentially other ways in which we could do this.

For example, we could enter into a partnership agreement with a hotel under which the hotel books Bolt journeys for their guests (introducer services) and in exchange of this service we would pay the hotel a certain percentage of the journey fee (commission). Very high level requirements list:

{noformat}Should be able to support multiple endpoints per SR cluster (e.g. k8s service + ingress)
Subjects should have configurable prefix and a unique base name (with a default value something like sre-e2e-monitoring + hash or constantly increasing counter, to simplify further cleanup ). We can create subjects not too often, e.g. once every 15 minutes or so, and publish new schema versions in between under already existing subject.
Updates to be made every 5 seconds. flow -> pause -> flow
The flow is: Publish new schema -> read it -> compare to ensure there is no data corruption
Old subjects should be periodically removed. Maybe once every hour or so.
Should expose metrics about deletion success/failure + latency. Most probably subject name shouldn't be included in labels, since it will bring high cardinality eventually. Better to have it somewhere in logs and investigate if needed. Good labels might be:
  1. cluster name (could be taken from k8s label)
  2. endpoint type (internal/external)
  3. endpoint name{noformat}

h3. Reasons for this Error:

# *Incorrect CVV*: The three-digit (or four-digit for American Express) CVV code may have been entered incorrectly.
# *Card Mismatch*: The card information entered does not align with the CVV code on the card.
# *Fraud Prevention*: Some card issuers may decline the transaction as a precaution if they detect discrepancies.
# *Expired Card*: If the card is expired, this error could also appear, though it usually results in a different error code.
# *Card Issuer Policy*: Some banks or card issuers may enforce strict CVV matching for all transactions.

Could you please ask the customer to check with their bank?

Technical test is also user-facing, but it’s purpose and approach towards users is a bit different.



For a technical test:

* The sample size is very small to use the few customers as ‘guinea pigs’ to validate whether *the system works properly* (can the backend handle the load, no big issues or bugs come up from the system error logs - we rely on our internal data rather than expecting customers to come and provide feedback)
* users do not get any in-app stories or comms that anything has even changed, people in the testing (treatment) group just sort of find the functionality and if they want, they can interract with it (and if they do, the system monitors the system behaviour).
* if some issues are caught, then it can happen several times that the test is stopped - additional development made - another technical test begins, etc, until all system errors or problems are fixed and after which the AB testing begins.


For AB testing:

* larger testing group to get data that has statistical significance
* usually focused on testing the user experience and behavior to see whether the *feature brings the expected value* in the long run from both user and company perspective
* here usually CXA also comes into play to gather any user experience details from support tickets.



We haven’t really discussed action items/steps for technical test vs AB testing from Program Management perspective (which I will bring up and try to sort out for future reference), but my own logic sort of says that for technical tests, maybe as a general rule (maybe I’d put an exception here for Safety 🤔) the process updates or articles don’t need to be published or announced to CS because:

* technical tests can start and end very quickly depending on the statistics
* the treatment group size is very small and likely has very little (if any) impact to CS tickets
* announcing updates about any technical test to CS agents can cause additional noise to an already busy channel and people not being able to keep up with everything.



In the current case, I think the MM changes in the Safety flow that were made, could be announced to MM CS (if they haven’t been already - I don’t have access to MM channels myself). 

But the ‘I can’t log in' updates for phase 1, it’s something I’d leave to be published and announced around where the AB testing begins.

{{driver_order_event_queue}} *table usage*

*About the feature*

[https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/FRAUD-2050|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/FRAUD-2050|smart-link] 

{{fraud-action /internal/fraud/rideHailing/batchNotifyOfDriverOrderFraudLater}}

The feature is used by {{ridehailing_driver_quality_check}} [checkpoint|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/rules?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22checkpoint_type%22%3A%22ridehailing_driver_quality_check%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] to send event to Driver Quality team regarding driver behavior.

Likely, this check is invoked when user cancel order. This is the way to provide information to Driver Quality service to adjust driver score in cases like “driver not moving”, “driver moving in wrong direction”

*Fraud implementation*

Fraud publishes events into {{driver-fraud-order-event}} SNS topic. {{DriverOrderEventPublisher}} is used which extends {{MqDbSimplePublisher}}

{{MqDbSimplePublisher}} implements reliable MQ architecture #3 [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/222035969/Message+queue+architectures#Architecture-%233%3A-Sending-order-state-change-events.-(reliable)|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/222035969/Message+queue+architectures#Architecture-%233%3A-Sending-order-state-change-events.-(reliable)|smart-link] 

This reliable architecture uses DB table.

However, it is not fully clear for me if we need reliable architecture here. The only useful property of this architecture for us - is that the table can collect messages (as cache) while MQ is not available. However, in case DB is unavailable → then events are lost.

Important: We don’t use this table as data source - there are no SELECT queries involved in business logic.

*MqDbSimplePublisher implementation*

Initialization:

* {{new DriverOrderEventPublisher(new AwsSnsMqPublisher(), db)}} [github|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/c10f073883cccacec775dbe2e07f80a09630c811/src/platform/commerce/fraud_action/main/action/Bootstrap.ts#L150] - creates instance
* {{await driverFraudEventPublisher.initCron(ctx)}} [github|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/c10f073883cccacec775dbe2e07f80a09630c811/src/platform/commerce/fraud_action/main/action/Bootstrap.ts#L319] - initializes CRON

Usage:

* {{await this.publisher.sendDriverOrderFraudNotification(...)}} [github|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/a72c12518ffa9e3b4868327d3bcdcab3e4451a46/src/platform/commerce/fraud_action/main/action/service/ridehailing/RideHailingOrderPublishService.ts#L19]

A call to [MqDbSimplePublisher.sendInTransaction()|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-nodejs-common/blob/05ff183c4b9978ffca1fbdd2bef7bda5cbb06850/src/async/mq/publish/db/MqDbPublisher.ts#L103] just inserts an event into configured table with {{waiting}} state.

Note: {{MqDbSimplePublisher}} requires a table with specific columns to be created. Note sure if required table definition is described anywhere.

Then there a CRON running. CRON implementation can be found [here|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-nodejs-common/blob/05ff183c4b9978ffca1fbdd2bef7bda5cbb06850/src/async/mq/publish/db/MqDbPublisher.ts#L148-L154]

The CRON:

* SELECTs rows with {{waiting}} state
* Send messages to MQ in batches
* UPDATEs or DELETEs rows corresponding to sent messages afterwards

*Suggested solution for cleaning*

# Clean all records with created older than 2024-11-22. The [table|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/2f1cb6dcfaa4a960b25bd409ee2a7c60784e742c/src/platform/commerce/fraud_action/db/taxify_fraud_action.t5.db.sql#L107-L119] has index by {{created}}
# Add {{delete_after_sent:true}} ( {{MqDbPublisherConfig}} ) to {{MqDbSimplePublisher}} constructor
## Thus, cron will delete sent events instead of updating them

At specific moment of time there are only few (1-10) rows with “waiting” state in the table. So, table size should reduce from 180 GiB to less than 100 KiB.

Later:

I would even consider to push events directly to MQ. Seems #3 MQ architecture is needed when we want to keep sent messages consistent with some updates to business tables. MQ is reliable enough to send events without tables. (Events doesn’t look critically important). There is bigger chance that fraud checkpoint which provides data will be unavailable, then MQ.

However, this requires more efforts. So, we can postpone it.

* Query to pivot all activities:
{noformat}with base as (
    select
        p.email,
        from_unixtime(hr.start_time) AS hour_start,
        from_unixtime(hr.end_time) AS hour_end,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'scheduled_seconds_total' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_scheduled_total,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'actual_seconds_worked' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_worked,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'scheduled_seconds_productive' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_scheduled_productive,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'actual_all_seconds_worked' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_worked_all,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'actual_utilization' THEN hr.value END) AS utilization_actual,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'schedule_adherence_percentage' THEN hr.value END) AS schedule_adherence_percentage,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'scheduled_seconds_bpo' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_scheduled_bpo,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'utilization' THEN hr.value END) AS utilization_planned,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'conformance_percentage' THEN hr.value END) AS conformance,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'adherence_percentage' THEN hr.value END) AS adherence_percentage,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'actual_utilization_all_channels' THEN hr.value END) AS utilization_actual_all,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'in_office_shrinkage' THEN hr.value END) AS in_office_shrinkage,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'seconds_in_adherence' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_in_adherence,
        MAX(CASE WHEN hr.name = 'actual_seconds_in_adherence_bpo' THEN hr.value END) AS seconds_in_adherence_actual_bpo
    from ng_fivetran_cs_assembled.hourly_report_metric hr
    join ng_fivetran_cs_assembled.people p
        on hr.agent_id = p.agent_id
    where hr.type = 'interval'
    group by p.email, from_unixtime(hr.start_time), from_unixtime(hr.end_time)
)


select * from base
limit 100;{noformat}
* Based on result, here are the formulas for main metrics:
** utilization_actual = seconds_worked / seconds_scheduled_total
** utilization_planned = seconds_scheduled_productive / seconds_scheduled_total
** conformance = seconds_worked / seconds_scheduled_productive
** adherence_percentage = seconds_in_adherence / seconds_scheduled_productive
* Done some testing, above aligns with Assembled :partying_face:

# *Selfie liveness check -* checks if selfie is a real picture of a person’s face and *not* a picture of picture or a picture of a screen.
# *Face match check (AWS)* - between the selfie and the uploaded document.
# *Document authenticity check (Veriff)* - making sure the document is not fake and extracts the data fields from it.
# *Document validity check* - ensures that the document is part of the list of supported documents and is not expired.
# *Duplicate user check -* (1) By document type, country and document number matching; (2) By document country and national identity number matching; (3) By full name fuzzy matching and date of birth matching. All of the rules above can be combined.

We don’t receive nor store any numerical representation of the face in any of these checks. Verification team confirmed that biometrics are only involved at stage 5 - *face match check*. AWS Rekognition provides a stateless CompareFaces API, which we use in order to determine how similar are the faces in the two images (we receive *similarity score*). The API that we use doesn’t store biometric data.

* Based on the current implementation of {{delivery-eater-data-store}} & {{delivery-provider-search}}:

** the {{limit}} parameter is used on the {{"/internal/searchProvidersInUserRange"}} , but this case is covered since each document is scored by ES

** also, based on the current logic on how the {{limit}} value that is sent to {{eater-data-store}} is computed, if there are filters involved (tags as well), the limit will be {{undefined}} ([https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/b51a16134cdbdfacae16cf147e7b08431bea5d02/src/delivery/eater/delivery_provider_search/main/service/provider/utils/SearchProvidersUtils.ts#L16|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/b51a16134cdbdfacae16cf147e7b08431bea5d02/src/delivery/eater/delivery_provider_search/main/service/provider/utils/SearchProvidersUtils.ts#L16] )

*The way I understand the issue/new process:*

The new policy for rider compensation will focus on two main criteria: the fraud check result and the user’s refund history. Verification of the reported issue will only occur when the fraud check result is inconclusive, meaning compensation could be denied even if evidence supports the user’s claim, based on their suspicious refund history.

*So - what could generally be problematic with this from a privacy standpoint?*

* It's critical to clearly define what constitutes "suspicious refund history." Does it mean an excessive number of unfounded refund requests? Have we documented or established a clear standard for *what is considered to be suspicious* in this case?
* Since the decision will determine whether a user gets a refund, will users be given an opportunity to contest the decision? For example, if Alfred denies a refund but the claim is valid (e.g., the ride truly didn’t happen), *can users challenge the outcome and eventually get refunded?*
* While this activity may not qualify as automated decision-making under GDPR due to the limited significance of its effect, to avoid restrictions, it’s *strongly recommended to have a process for escalating cases to a human reviewer (i.e. CS)*, at least upon user request.

I don’t see any significant risks with this process, but *ensuring fairness* is crucial. Automating for efficiency is perfectly acceptable, but we must ensure that our *rules are unbiased and do not result in false positives* when determining a user's eligibility for a refund.
